Claude’s free plan trains on pasted data by default—flip one switch to stop it. Most users never check, and sensitive customer info stays in their system for 30 days. Here’s how to opt out in under two minutes.
#aitoolsforbusiness #aiforbusiness #marketingaudit #irishsmallbusiness
carousels.hook: Claude’s free plan trains on every paste by default
carousels.throughline: Claude’s free plan automatically trains on pasted data unless you opt out—here’s how to stop it and protect your customer information.

reel_beats.hook: You’re training Claude for free—with your customer data

body.text: Claude’s free plan uses every paste to train its AI, so your customer emails and order details stay in their system for 30 days.
It’s on by default, so most users never notice—and their sensitive data gets stored without permission.
This costs you privacy, not money, but the fix takes 60 seconds—one toggle in settings.
Open settings, flip ‘Improve Claude’ off, and avoid pasting anything sensitive until you do.

screen.title: Stop Claude training on your data
screen.mechanism: Flipping this switch stops Claude from using your pasted data to train its AI—paid plans never train on inputs.

reel_beats.send_line: Send this to whoever runs your AI tools

body_slides.text: Open Claude’s settings from the top-right menu—it’s under ‘Data & Privacy.’
Find the toggle labeled ‘Improve Claude with your data’—it’s on by default.
Flip it off to stop Claude from training on anything you paste.
Past inputs stay for 30 days unless you delete chats.
Avoid pasting customer emails, phone numbers, or order details.
Use Claude’s paid plan for sensitive data—it never trains on inputs.

Gmail’s Primary tab opens for emails with replies—not clever subject lines. One reply moves your email in, two lock it for future sends, and a sender score above 90 skips spam entirely. Here’s what actually decides where your email lands.
#emailmarketingtips #emaildeliverability #leadgeneration #galwaybusiness
carousels.hook: Gmail moves emails to Primary after one reply
carousels.throughline: Gmail’s Primary tab prioritizes engagement over subject lines—here’s how replies, opens, and sender score actually decide where your email lands.

reel_beats.hook: Gmail buries your email unless someone replies

body.text: Gmail’s Primary tab only opens for emails that get replies—subject lines are just the first hurdle.
After one reply, Gmail moves your email to Primary and keeps it there for future sends.
This costs you opens—emails in Primary get 43% more views than those in Promotions.
Ask one person to reply, then watch your open rate climb without changing a word.

chart.label: open rate boost
chart.caption: Emails in Primary get 43% more opens than those in Promotions—one reply moves them there.

reel_beats.send_line: Send this to your email marketer

body_slides.text: One reply moves your email to Primary—even with a generic subject line.
After the first open, Gmail tracks engagement instead of subject lines.
A sender score above 90 skips the spam filter entirely.
Emails with replies get 43% more opens in Primary than those without.
Gmail ignores ‘urgent’ or ‘free’ in subject lines if your sender score is high.
Two replies lock your email in Primary for future sends.

Google Ads wastes 30% of your budget on browsers—one report shows which searches never convert. Sort by conversions, add wasteful searches as negatives, and cut wasted spend by 30% without touching your budget. Here’s how to do it in 5 minutes.
#googleadstips #ppcmanagement #searchads #irishbusiness
carousels.hook: Google Ads wastes 30% of your budget on browsers
carousels.throughline: Google Ads charges the same for browsers and buyers—here’s how to find and exclude the searches that waste your budget.

reel_beats.hook: Google Ads burns 30% of your budget on searches that never buy

body.text: Google Ads charges the same for a search that bounces and one that converts, so wasteful searches drain your budget.
The Search terms report shows which searches actually lead to sales—and which just waste money.
This costs you 30% of your budget on average—without you even noticing.
Sort by conversions, add wasteful searches as negatives, and watch your cost per lead drop.

chart.label: wasted spend cut
chart.caption: Adding negative keywords cuts wasted spend by 30%—without reducing your ad budget.

reel_beats.send_line: Send this to whoever runs your ads

body_slides.text: Open the ‘Search terms’ report under ‘Keywords’ in your dashboard.
Sort by conversions to see which searches actually lead to sales.
Look for searches with zero conversions but high spend—these are browsers.
Add these as negative keywords to stop Google from showing your ad for them.
Check this weekly—new wasteful searches pop up as trends change.
This cuts wasted spend by 30% on average without touching your budget.

carousels.hook: Gmail’s spam filter skips ‘urgent’ if your sender score is high
carousels.throughline: Gmail’s spam filter ignores ‘urgent’ in subject lines—here’s what actually decides whether your email gets opened or buried.

reel_beats.hook: Gmail ignores ‘urgent’ in your subject line if your sender score is high

body.text: Gmail’s spam filter looks at sender score first—subject lines are a distant second.
A score above 90 skips the spam filter entirely, no matter what your subject says.
This saves you from spam—emails with high sender scores get opened 43% more often.
Focus on building sender trust, not clever subject lines, and watch your open rate climb.

chart.label: open rate boost
chart.caption: Emails with a sender score above 90 get opened 43% more often—subject lines don’t matter as much.

reel_beats.send_line: Send this to your email marketer

body_slides.text: Gmail’s spam filter checks sender score first—subject lines come second.
A score above 90 skips the spam filter entirely.
‘Urgent’ or ‘free’ in subject lines only flags emails with low sender scores.
One reply moves your email to Primary—Gmail prioritizes engagement.
Subject lines matter for the first open—after that, Gmail tracks replies.
Focus on sender trust—it’s the only thing Gmail’s spam filter cares about.
